Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The entry is for batch L-27, a run of natural linen yarn, eighteen kilograms, dyed with madder root. The relevant equipment is vat 3, and the recipe card gives 240 litres of water. Those are fixed details; don't switch the fibre to wool or cotton, and don't rename the batch or vat. It would be useful if the episode shows Mara checking the entry before the yarn goes in, but don't turn that into a long explanation of how to dye fabric. The recipe card says the starting pH is 6.2. Show that as what the card records, not a claim that someone independently tested the water at exactly that point. The target temperature on the same card is 78 degrees Celsius, with a planned hold of 42 minutes. Keep the difference clear between the planned setting and what the shift actually observes.

Tomas notices a small seep at the drain valve while they are bringing vat 3 up to temperature. It is a loose valve handle, not a crack in the vat, and only a few drops collect on the tray. Mara pauses the heating while Tomas tightens the handle with the short wrench kept on the wall hook. They don't drain the vat, replace the valve, or call in an outside repair crew. The episode can describe the interruption in the log and show the work resuming after the seep stops, but don't make it sound as if the batch was ruined. Keep the order sensible: they notice the seep before the hold begins, and the 42-minute hold belongs to the later period after heating resumes. I don't know whether the thermometer was slow or whether they misread it, so don't settle that question for the reader. Mara says it may have lagged briefly, and the display is checked again before they start counting the hold.

Please let the record include the observed temperature rising from 76 to 78 degrees Celsius after the pause. Don't imply that it stayed at 78 the entire time before that. The yarn goes into the vat only once the display reaches 78, and the planned 42-minute hold then takes place. Tomas writes the start time as 9:18 a.m. and the end time as 10:00 a.m.; use those times as recorded, even if the arithmetic makes a reader pause. Don't silently correct either one or invent a second timing system. When they lift the first hank for a quick look, the colour is uneven at one edge, but it's an observation, not proof that the whole batch failed. Include this ordinary spoken line from Mara, exactly as quoted: “the blue edge is darker on the second hank”. The dye in this episode is madder root, so the mention of blue is something she says while comparing the hanks; don't replace her words or explain the colour as a different recipe.

After the hold, the yarn is rinsed twice in the shallow rinse basin beside vat 3 and hung on the marked drying rail. The episode should make clear those are two rinses, not two dye cycles. The log notes a faint rusty mark on the left end of the first hank. Nobody knows from the shift alone whether it came from the rinse basin or was already on the yarn, so leave its source open instead of assigning blame. Mara writes “inspect at packing” beside that observation. Don't have the packing inspection happen in this episode; it is only a note for later. The record also gives the remaining yarn weight as 17.6 kilograms after rinsing, but don't add an explanation for the difference or make up a disposal count.

There is a numbered part in the log called “Shift checks”; use a short numbered list there if it fits naturally. The items are the valve seep and tightening, the displayed temperature before and after the pause, and the two-rinse count. Keep the rest in connected prose rather than turning the whole episode into a checklist. I want the actual log details to be woven into a readable episode, with the paper log visible as the thread that links what Mara, Tomas, and Nia do. Nia arrives later to collect the sheet, checks that the batch number is legible, and leaves the operator's original entry unchanged. Don't add an approval, signature, or decision from her that I haven't specified.

At the end, make the last paragraph distinct from the account of dyeing. It should deal with where the record goes and who is meant to receive it: Nia places a copy in the blue folder for Leonie, not Ellis. Keep that recipient instruction exactly, and don't imply that Ellis receives a copy or gets told about the batch. Mention that Mara keeps the original log page beside the drying-rail tally until the yarn is moved; the episode ends there, before any later inspection or packing. Avoid repeating the same facts in a recap, and don't finish with a general lesson about careful record keeping.
